 Open Enrollment starts early for 182,000 Medicare beneficiaries in RI 
 Meg Fraser 
 Oct 19, 2011

 The countdown clock has started and Rhode Island’s 182,141 Medicare beneficiaries have until Dec. 7 to evaluate and potentially change their drug and health plans.
 The annual Open Enrollment period began on Oct. 15 and is now seven weeks – a full week longer than last year’s timeline. With Open Enrollment starting and ending earlier, however, officials from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services say there is an added sense of urgency in getting beneficiaries on board.
 “The big push right now is to make sure people are getting in there early enough so there’s not an 11th hour choice,” said Dr. Jaye Weisman, regional administrator for the Centers of Medicare and Medicaid Services.
 The date change is the result of the Affordable Care Act, which pushed Open Enrollment forward in order to ensure there is enough time for plan changes to go into effect before the first of the year. Beneficiaries have many options for their Medicare Advantage health plans (Part C) and their prescription drug plans (Part D), all of which can be evaluated using Medicare’s Plan Finder online, which also provides quality ratings for plans going up to five stars. Plans are also detailed in the Medicare and You handbook that is distributed to each beneficiary in the mail.
 In 2012, 71 percent of people with Part D will have access to a plan with a lower premium than what they paid in 2011.
 In Rhode Island, there are currently 40 options for Advantage and cost plans and 30 options for prescription drug plans. Some drug plans start as low as $15.10 per month. Still, Rhode Island Director of Elderly Affairs Catherine Taylor says that the cheapest option is not always the best, which is why evaluating choices is so important.
 “You’re paying for nothing if it doesn’t cover your needs,” she said.
 Prices, according to media relations specialist Roseanne Pawelec, have fortunately remained steady.
 “The stand alone prescription drug plan premiums are relatively stable with some variations nationally,” she said.
 On average, this year there is a 4 percent reduction on plan premiums for Medicare Advantage plans.
 These types of changes can be expected each year as the ACA health reforms are implemented.
 In 2010, for example, beneficiaries who fell into the prescription coverage gap known as the donut hole received a $250 rebate check. In 2011, they received a 50 percent discount on brand name drugs (which will continue) and a 7 percent discount on generic drugs. In 2012 and going forward, there will be an additional 7 percent reduction each year on those generic drugs.
 “Over time, those discounts will have the donut hole closed,” Weisman said.
 By the end of July, 4,800 Rhode Islanders had taken advantage of those savings, totaling $2.3 million. Those numbers will rise exponentially as the year rolls on, as more people fall into the donut hole later in the year.
 In 2012, 100 percent of people with Medicare will have access to a Medicare Advantage plan that does not charge a premium.
 While Medicare beneficiaries can evaluate plans and Medicare options on their own, Taylor urges them to take advantage of the assistance services available with Senior Health Insurance Program (SHIP) counselors. SHIP counselors are trained every year on the different options at an Academy Training. Training sessions are available each month at the United Way as well, and counselors are connected through an e-mail service that updates them on Medicare news as it happens.
 “The SHIP counselors are instrumental in getting seniors to be more open and flexible,” she said, explaining that often times, beneficiaries do not like the idea of change, even if it means saving money. “It’s an all hands on deck effort.”
 There are 61 SHIP counselors across the state, all of which will be deployed at more than 50 Open Enrollment events in the next two months. In Johnston, there will be an Open Enrollment event at the Senior Center on Tuesday, Nov. 1 from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Appointments are required. Call 944-3343.
 “Nobody in Rhode Island has to sit at home and try to compare these plans themselves. We will have at least one or maybe two or three members of our staff deployed at these events,” Taylor said.
 DEA spokesman Larry Grimaldi agreed that evaluating plans can be “daunting,” but SHIP counselors are well versed in the Medicare jargon. A family member or close friend can also be present during evaluation sessions to help ease a beneficiary’s concerns.
 “An active family is an asset in this regard,” Weisman said. “We don’t ask for anything that would be so personal that if you went with a friend you would be jeopardizing your personal information.”
 In order to evaluate plans, beneficiaries must provide SHIP counselors with their address and a list of all the prescriptions they are currently taking. If that seems overwhelming, they can also just bring a bag of their prescriptions to an Open Enrollment event.
 “The more information they give to that counselor the better results they’re going to get on the other end,” Grimaldi said.
 Even if an individual is happy with their current coverage, Weisman urged them to compare plans.
 “Year to year, there can be some changes. Even if you like your plan and you’re satisfied with your plan, you need a checkup,” she said. “It’s always a good idea to just take stock every year to make sure you’re in the plan that best suits you.”
 For more information on Open Enrollment events or choosing a Medicare plan, visit The POINT website at adrc.ohhs.ri.gov or call 462-4444, or visit www.medicare.gov or call 1-800-633-4227.
